parts.text:
Express

$\dfrac{3x+5}{x^2+x-12}-\dfrac{2}{x-3}$

as a single fraction in its simplest form.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $x^2+x-12=(x+4)(x-3)$, correctly factorised. It could appear anywhere in their solution.
M1: Attempt as a single fraction $\dfrac{(3x+5)(x-3)-2(x^2+x-12)}{(x^2+x-12)(x-3)}$ or $\dfrac{3x+5-2(x+4)}{(x+4)(x-3)}$. For an attempt to combine two fractions. The denominator must be correct for 'their' fractions. The terms could be separate but one term must have been modified. Condone invisible brackets.
A1: Correct unsimplified answer $\dfrac{x-3}{(x+4)(x-3)}$
A1: cao $\dfrac{1}{(x+4)}$. Do not isw in this question.
Note: The method of partial fractions is perfectly acceptable and can score full marks: $\dfrac{3x+5}{(x+4)(x-3)}-\dfrac{2}{x-3}=\dfrac{1}{x+4}+\dfrac{2}{x-3}-\dfrac{2}{x-3}=\dfrac{1}{x+4}$.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Examples of work scoring this mark are; $\dfrac{(3x+5)(x-3)}{(x^2+x-12)(x-3)}-\dfrac{2(x^2+x-12)}{(x^2+x-12)(x-3)}$ Two separate terms; $\dfrac{3x+5-2x+4}{(x+4)(x-3)}$ Single term, invisible bracket; $\dfrac{(3x+5)}{(x^2+x-12)(x-3)}-\dfrac{2(x^2+x-12)}{(x^2+x-12)(x-3)}$ Separate terms, only one numerator modified
- If $\dfrac{x^2-6x-9}{(x^2+x-12)(x-3)}$ scored M1 the fraction must be subsequently be reduced to a correct $\dfrac{x-3}{x^2+x-12}$ or $\dfrac{(x-3)(x-3)}{(x+4)(x-3)(x-3)}$ to score this mark.

questions.stem:
Figure 1 shows a sketch of the curve with equation $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$, $x > 0$, where f is an increasing function of $x$. The curve crosses the $x$-axis at the point $(1, 0)$ and the line $x = 0$ is an asymptote to the curve.

On separate diagrams, sketch the curve with equation

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Correct shape. Look for an increasing function with decreasing gradient. Condone linear looking functions in the first quadrant. It needs to look asymptotic at the $y$ axis and have no obvious maximum point. It must be wholly contained in quadrants 1 and 4.
B1: Crosses $x$-axis at $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0\right)$. Accept $\dfrac{1}{2}$, 0.5 or even $\left(0,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ marked on the correct axis. There must be a graph for this mark to be scored.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Indicate clearly on each sketch the coordinates of the point at which the curve crosses or meets the $x$-axis.
(b) $y = |\mathrm{f}(x)|$, $x > 0$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Correct shape wholly contained in quadrant 1. The shape to the rhs of the cusp must not have an obvious maximum. Accept linear, or positive with decreasing gradient. The gradient of the curve to the lhs of the cusp/minimum should always be negative. The curve in this section should not 'bend' back past $(1,0)$ forming a 'C' shape or have incorrect curvature.
B1: The curve touches or crosses the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$. Allow for the curve passing through a point marked '1' on the $x$-axis. Condone the point marked on the correct axis as $(0,1)$.
B1: Award for a cusp, not a minimum at $(1,0)$.
Note: $\mathrm{f}(|x|)$ scores B0 B1 B0 under the scheme. If the graphs are not labelled (a) and (b), then they are to be marked in the order they are presented.

questions.stem:
$\mathrm{f}(x) = 7\cos x + \sin x$

Given that $\mathrm{f}(x) = R\cos(x-\alpha)$, where $R > 0$ and $0 < \alpha < 90°$,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find the exact value of $R$ and the value of $\alpha$ to one decimal place.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $R=\sqrt{50}$. Accept $5\sqrt2$. Accept $R=\pm\sqrt{50}$. Do not accept $R=\sqrt{(7^2+1^2)}$ or the decimal equivalent 7.07… unless you see $\sqrt{50}$ or $5\sqrt2$ as well.
M1: For $\tan\alpha=\pm\dfrac{1}{7}$ or $\tan\alpha=\pm\dfrac{7}{1}$. Condone if this comes from $\cos\alpha=7,\sin\alpha=1$. If $R$ is used then only accept $\sin\alpha=\pm\dfrac{1}{R}$ or $\cos\alpha=\pm\dfrac{7}{R}$.
A1: $\alpha=$ awrt $8.1$. Be aware that $\tan\alpha=7\Rightarrow\alpha=81.9$ can easily be mistaken for the correct answer. Note that the radian answer awrt $0.1418…$ is A0.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Hence solve the equation

$7\cos x + \sin x = 5$

for $0 \leqslant x < 360°$, giving your answers to one decimal place.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: For using their answers to part (a) and moving from $R\cos(x\pm\alpha)=5\Rightarrow\cos(x\pm\alpha)=\dfrac{5}{R}$ using their numerical values of $R$ and $\alpha$. This may be implied for sight of 53.1 if $R$ and $\alpha$ were correct.
M1: For achieving $x\pm\alpha=$ awrt $45°$ or $315$, leading to one value of $x$ in the range. Note that for this to be scored $R$ has to be correct (to 2sf) as awrt 45, 315 must be achieved. This may be implied for achieving an answer of either $45+$ their $\alpha$ or $315+$ their $\alpha$.
A1: One correct answer, either awrt $53.1°$ or $323.1°$.
M1: For an attempt at finding a secondary value of $x$ in the range. Usually this is an attempt at solving $x-$ their $8.1°=360°-$ their $45°\Rightarrow x=..$
A1: Both values correct awrt $53.1°$ and $323.1°$. Withhold this mark if there are extra values in the range. Ignore extra values outside the range.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Answers all in radians. Lose the first time that it appears but demand an accuracy of 2dp. Part (a) $R=\sqrt{50}$ $\alpha=awrt\ 0.14$ Part (b) $x=awrt\ 0.927,\ 5.64$. Accuracy must be to 3 sf. With correct working this would score (a) B1M1A0 (b) M1A1A1M1A1. Mixed degrees and radians refer to the main scheme

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) State the values of $k$ for which the equation

$7\cos x + \sin x = k$

has only one solution in the interval $0 \leqslant x < 360°$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:

A1ft: Both values $k=\pm\sqrt{50}$ oe. Follow through on their numerical $R$.

questions.stem:
The functions f and g are defined by

$\mathrm{f}: x \mapsto 2|x| + 3$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$,

$\mathrm{g}: x \mapsto 3 - 4x$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) State the range of f.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempt at calculating f at $x=0$. Sight of 3 is sufficient. Accept $\mathrm{f}(x)>3$ and $x>3$ for M1.
A1: $\mathrm{f}(x)\geqslant 3$. Accept $y\geqslant3$, range$\geqslant3$, $[3,\infty)$. Do not accept $\mathrm{f}(x)>3$, $x\geqslant3$. The correct answer is sufficient for both marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find $\mathrm{fg}(1)$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: A full method of finding $\mathrm{fg}(1)$. The order of substituting into the expressions must be correct and $2|x|+3$ must be used as opposed to $2x+3$. Accept an attempt to calculate $2|x|+3$ when $x=-1$. Accept an attempt to put $x=1$ into $3-4x$ and then substituting their answer to $3-4x|_{x=1}$ into $2|x|+3$. Do not accept the substitution of $x=1$ into $2|x|+3$, followed by their result into '3-4x'. This is evidence of incorrect order.
A1: $\mathrm{fg}(1)=5$. Watch for $1\xrightarrow{3-4x}1\xrightarrow{2|x|+3}5$ which is M1A0.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find $\mathrm{g}^{-1}$, the inverse function of g.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Award for an attempt to make $x$ or a swapped $y$ the subject of the formula. It must be a full method and cannot finish $4x=..$. You can condone at most one 'arithmetic' error for this method mark.
A1: Obtaining a correct expression $\mathrm{g}^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3-x}{4}$ oe such as $\mathrm{g}^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x-3}{-4}$, $\mathrm{g}^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{x}{4}$. It must be in terms of $x$, but could be expressed 'y=' or $\mathrm{g}^{-1}(x)\to$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $y=3-4x\Rightarrow4x=3+y\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3+y}{4}$ is fine for the M1 as there is only one error. $y=3-4x\Rightarrow4x=3-y\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3}{4}-y$ is fine for the M1 as there is only one error. $y=3-4x\Rightarrow4x=3+y\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3}{4}+y$ is M0 as there are two arithmetic errors

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Solve the equation

$\mathrm{gg}(x) + [\mathrm{g}(x)]^2 = 0$
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Sight of $[\mathrm{g}(x)]^2=(3-4x)^2$. If only the expanded version appears it must be correct.
M1: A full attempt to find $\mathrm{gg}(x)=3-4(3-4x)$. Condone invisible brackets. Note that it may appear in an equation.
A1: $16x^2-8x=0$. Accept other alternatives such as $2x^2=x$.
M1: For factorising their quadratic or cancelling their $Ax^2=Bx$ by $x$ to get $\geqslant1$ value of $x$. If they have a 3TQ then usual methods are applicable.
A1: Both values correct $x=0, 0.5$ oe.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Differentiate

$\dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sqrt{x}}$

with respect to $x$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Award for the sight of $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos 2x)=-2\sin 2x$. This could be seen in their differential.
M1: Applies $\dfrac{vu'-uv'}{v^2}$ to $\dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sqrt{x}}$. There must have been some attempt to differentiate both terms. If the rule is quoted it must be correct. If the rule is not quoted (nor implied by their working, with terms written out u=…,u'=…,v=…,v'=….followed by their $\dfrac{vu'-uv'}{v^2}$) then only accept answers of the form $\dfrac{\sqrt{x}\times\pm A\sin 2x-\cos 2x\times Bx^{-\frac{1}{2}}}{(\sqrt{x})^2}$ or $x^{\frac14}$.
A1: Award for a correct answer. This does not need to be simplified. $=\dfrac{-2\sqrt{x}\sin 2x-\frac12 x^{-\frac12}\cos 2x}{x}$
Alt using product rule accepted, same mark allocation.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Alt (a) using the product rule. M1 Applies $vu'+uv'$ to $x^{-\frac12}\cos2x$. If the rule is quoted it must be correct. There must have been some attempt to differentiate both terms. If the rule is not quoted (nor implied by their working, with terms written out u=…,u'=….,v=….,v'=….followed by their $vu'+uv'$) then only accept answers of the form $\pm Ax^{-\frac12}\sin2x-Bx^{-\frac32}\cos2x$. A1 Award for a correct answer. This does not need to be simplified. $-2x^{-\frac12}\sin2x-\frac12x^{-\frac32}\cos2x$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec^2 3x)$ can be written in the form

$\mu(\tan 3x + \tan^3 3x)$

where $\mu$ is a constant.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Award for a correct application of the chain rule on $\sec^2 3x$. Sight of $C\sec 3x\sec 3x\tan 3x$ is sufficient.
dM1: Replacing $\sec^2 3x=1+\tan^2 3x$ in their derivative to create an expression in just $\tan 3x$. It is dependent upon the first M being scored.
A1: The correct answer $6(\tan 3x+\tan^3 3x)$. There is no need to write $\mu=6$.
Alternative methods using product rule, or $\sec 3x=\frac{1}{\cos 3x}$, or $\sec^2 3x=1+\tan^2 3x$ from the start are acceptable with the same mark allocation, leading to $6(\tan 3x+\tan^3 3x)$.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Alt (b) using the product rule. M1 Writes $\sec^23x$ as $\sec3x\times\sec3x$ and uses the product rule with $u'=A\sec3x\tan3x$ and $v'=B\sec3x\tan3x$ to produce a derivative of the form $A\sec3x\tan3x\sec3x+B\sec3x\tan3x\sec3x$. dM1 Replaces $\sec^23x$ with $1+\tan^23x$ to produce an expression in just $\tan3x$. It is dependent upon the first M being scored.
- Alt (b) using $\sec3x=\frac{1}{\cos3x}$ and proceeding by the chain or quotient rule. M1 Writes $\sec^23x$ as $(\cos3x)^{-2}$ and differentiates to $A(\cos3x)^{-3}\sin3x$. Alternatively writes $\sec^23x$ as $\frac{1}{(\cos3x)^2}$ and achieves $\frac{(\cos3x)^2\times0-1\times A\cos3x\sin3x}{(\cos^23x)^2}$. dM1 Uses $\frac{\sin3x}{\cos3x}=\tan3x$ and $\frac{1}{\cos^23x}=\sec^23x$ and $\sec^23x=1+\tan^23x$ in their derivative to create an expression in just $\tan3x$. It is dependent upon the first M being scored.
- Alt (b) using $\sec^23x=1+\tan^23x$. M1 Writes $\sec^23x$ as $1+\tan^23x$ and uses chain rule to produce a derivative of the form $A\tan3x\sec^23x$ or the product rule to produce a derivative of the form $C\tan3x\sec^23x+D\tan3x\sec^23x$. dM1 Replaces $\sec^23x=1+\tan^23x$ to produce an expression in just $\tan3x$. It is dependent upon the first M being scored.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Given $x = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{y}{3}\right)$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ in terms of $x$, simplifying your answer.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Award for knowing the method that $\sin\left(\frac{y}{3}\right)$ differentiates to $\cos\left(\frac{y}{3}\right)$. The lhs does not need to be correct/present. Award for $2\sin\left(\frac{y}{3}\right)\to A\cos\left(\frac{y}{3}\right)$.
A1: $x=2\sin\left(\frac{y}{3}\right)\Rightarrow\dfrac{dx}{dy}=\dfrac23\cos\left(\frac{y}{3}\right)$. Both sides must be correct.
dM1: Award for inverting their $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ and using $\sin^2\frac{y}{3}+\cos^2\frac{y}{3}=1$ to produce an expression for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ in terms of $x$ only. It is dependent upon the first M1 being scored. An alternative to Pythagoras is a triangle.
A1: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}$ cao. Expression must be in its simplest form. Candidates who write $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{2\cos(\arcsin(x/2))}$ do not score the mark. BUT $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{1-\sin^2(\arcsin(x/2))}}$ does score M1 as they clearly use a correct Pythagorean identity as required by the notes. Do not accept $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{1-\frac14 x^2}}$ or $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\frac13\sqrt{4-x^2}}$ for the final A1.
Alt: Rearranging to $y=A\arcsin Bx$ and differentiating to $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{1-Bx^2}}$ (M1), as above but form of the rhs must be correct $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{C}{\sqrt{1-(x/2)^2}}$ (dM1), correct but unsimplified answer (A1), $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}$ (A1).

A1: Award for a correct answer. This does not need to be simplified. $=\dfrac{-2\sqrt{x}\sin 2x-\frac12 x^{-\frac12}\cos 2x}{x}$

questions.stem:
Figure 2 shows a sketch of part of the curve with equation $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ where

$\mathrm{f}(x) = (x^2+3x+1)\mathrm{e}^{x^2}$

The curve cuts the $x$-axis at points $A$ and $B$ as shown in Figure 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Calculate the $x$ coordinate of $A$ and the $x$ coordinate of $B$, giving your answers to 3 decimal places.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Solves $x^2+3x+1=0$ by completing the square or the formula, producing two 'non integer' answers. Do not accept factorisation here. Accept awrt $-0.4$ and $-2.6$ for this mark.
A1: Answers correct. Accept awrt $-0.382, -2.618$. Accept just the answers for both marks. Don't withhold the marks for incorrect labelling.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find $\mathrm{f}'(x)$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Applies the product rule $vu'+uv'$ to $(x^2+3x+1)\mathrm{e}^{x^2}$. If the rule is quoted it must be correct and there must have been some attempt to differentiate both terms. If the rule is not quoted (nor implied by their working, ie. terms are written out u=…,u'=…,v=…,v'=….followed by their $vu'+uv'$) only accept answers of the form $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=\mathrm{f}'(x)=\mathrm{e}^{x^2}(Ax+B)+(x^2+3x+1)Cx\mathrm{e}^{x^2}$
A1: One term of $\mathrm{f}'(x)=\mathrm{e}^{x^2}(2x+3)+(x^2+3x+1)\mathrm{e}^{x^2}\times2x$ correct. There is no need to simplify.
A1: A fully correct (unsimplified) answer $\mathrm{f}'(x)=\mathrm{e}^{x^2}(2x+3)+(x^2+3x+1)\mathrm{e}^{x^2}\times2x$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The curve has a minimum turning point at the point $P$ as shown in Figure 2.
(c) Show that the $x$ coordinate of $P$ is the solution of

$x = -\dfrac{3(2x^2+1)}{2(x^2+2)}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Sets their $\mathrm{f}'(x)=0$ and either factorises out, or cancels by $\mathrm{e}^{x^2}$ to produce a polynomial equation in $x$.
M1: Rearranges the cubic polynomial to $Ax^3+Bx=Cx^2+D$ and factorises to reach $x(Ax^2+B)=Cx^2+D$ or equivalent.
A1*: Correctly proceeds to $x=-\dfrac{3(2x^2+1)}{2(x^2+2)}$. This is a given answer.
Alt (working backwards): Moves correctly from $x=-\dfrac{3(2x^2+1)}{2(x^2+2)}$ to $2x^3+6x^2+4x+3=0$ (M1); states or implies that $\mathrm{f}'(x)=0$ (M1); makes a conclusion to tie up the argument, e.g. hence the minimum point occurs when $x=-\dfrac{3(2x^2+1)}{2(x^2+4)}$ (A1).

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Use the iteration formula

$x_{n+1} = -\dfrac{3(2x_n^2+1)}{2(x_n^2+2)}$, with $x_0 = -2.4$,

to calculate the values of $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$, giving your answers to 3 decimal places.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Sub $x_0=-2.4$ into $x_{n+1}=-\dfrac{3(2x_n^2+1)}{2(x_n^2+2)}$. This may be implied by awrt $-2.42$, or $x_{n+1}=-\dfrac{3(2\times-2.4^2+1)}{2(-2.4^2+2)}$
A1: Awrt $x_1=-2.420$. The subscript is not important. Mark as the first value given.
A1: awrt $x_2=-2.427$ awrt $x_3=-2.430$ The subscripts are not important. Mark as the second and third values given.

parts.label: e
parts.text:
The $x$ coordinate of $P$ is $\alpha$.
(e) By choosing a suitable interval, prove that $\alpha = -2.43$ to 2 decimal places.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
Note that continued iteration is not allowed.
M1: Sub $x=-2.425$ and $-2.435$ into $\mathrm{f}'(x)$, starts to compare signs and gets at least one correct to 1 sf rounded or truncated.
A1: Both values correct (1sf rounded or truncated), a reason and a minimal conclusion. Acceptable reasons are change in sign, positive and negative and $\mathrm{f}'(a)\times\mathrm{f}'(b)<0$. Minimal conclusions are hence $\alpha=-2.43$, hence shown, hence root.
Alt 1 (using adapted $\mathrm{f}'(x)$): Sub $x=-2.425$ and $-2.435$ into cubic part of $\mathrm{f}'(x)=2x^3+6x^2+4x+3$, starts to compare signs and gets at least one correct to 1sf rounded or truncated (M1); both values correct of adapted $\mathrm{f}'(x)$ correct (1sf rounded or truncated), a reason and a minimal conclusion (A1).
Alt 2 (using $\mathrm{f}(x)$): Sub $x=-2.425, -2.43$ and $-2.435$ into $\mathrm{f}(x)=(x^2+3x+1)\mathrm{e}^{x^2}$, starts to compare sizes and gets at least one correct to 4sf rounded (M1); all three values correct of $\mathrm{f}(x)$ correct (4sf rounded), a reason and a minimal conclusion, e.g. $\mathrm{f}(-2.43)<\mathrm{f}(-2.425)$, $\mathrm{f}(-2.43)<\mathrm{f}(-2.435)$, a sketch; minimal conclusions are hence $\alpha=-2.43$, hence shown, hence root (A1).
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\mathrm{f}'(-2.425)=+22.4,\ \mathrm{f}'(-2.435)=-15.02$ M1. Change in sign, hence $\mathrm{f}'(x)=0$ in between. Therefore $\alpha=-2.43$ (2dp) A1
- Alt 1 7(e): Adapted $\mathrm{f}'(-2.425)=+0.06,\ \mathrm{f}'(-2.435)=-0.04$ M1. Change in sign, hence $\mathrm{f}'(x)=0$ in between. Therefore $\alpha=-2.43$ (2dp) A1
- Alt 2 7(e): $\mathrm{f}(-2.425)=-141.2,\ \mathrm{f}(-2.435)=-141.2,\ \mathrm{f}(-2.43)=-141.3$ M1. $\mathrm{f}(-2.43)<\mathrm{f}(-2.425),\ \mathrm{f}(-2.43)<\mathrm{f}(-2.435)$. Therefore $\alpha=-2.43$ (2dp) A1

questions.stem:
Figure 3 shows the graph of $P$ against $t$.

The population of a town is being studied. The population $P$, at time $t$ years from the start of the study, is assumed to be

$P = \dfrac{8000}{1+7\mathrm{e}^{-kt}}$, $t \geqslant 0$,

where $k$ is a positive constant.

The graph of $P$ against $t$ is shown in Figure 3.

Use the given equation to

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find the population at the start of the study,
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Sets $t=0$, giving $\mathrm{e}^{-k\times0}=1$. Award if candidate attempts $\dfrac{8000}{1+7\times1}$, $\dfrac{8000}{8}$
A1: Correct answer only 1000. Accept 1000 for both marks as long as no incorrect working is seen.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) find a value for the expected upper limit of the population.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: 8000. Accept $P<8000$. Condone $P\leqslant8000$ but not $P>8000$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Given also that the population reaches 2500 at 3 years from the start of the study,

(c) calculate the value of $k$ to 3 decimal places.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Sets both $t=3$, and $P=2500\Rightarrow2500=\dfrac{8000}{1+7\mathrm{e}^{-3k}}$. This may be implied by a subsequent correct line.
M1: Rearranges the equation to make $\mathrm{e}^{\pm3k}$ the subject. They need to multiply by the $1+7\mathrm{e}^{-3k}$ term, and proceed to $\mathrm{e}^{\pm3k}=A$, $A>0$
A1: The correct intermediate answer of $\mathrm{e}^{-3k}=\dfrac{2.2}{7}, \dfrac{11}{35}$ or equivalent. Accept awrt $0.31..$. Alternatively accept $\mathrm{e}^{3k}=\dfrac{35}{11}, 3.18..$ or equivalent.
M1: Proceeds from $\mathrm{e}^{\pm3k}=A$, $A>0$ by correctly taking $\ln$'s and then making $k$ the subject of the formula. Award for $\mathrm{e}^{-3k}=A\Rightarrow-3k=\ln(A)\Rightarrow k=\dfrac{\ln(A)}{-3}$. If $\mathrm{e}^{3k}$ was found accept $\mathrm{e}^{3k}=C\Rightarrow3k=\ln C\Rightarrow k=\dfrac{\ln C}{3}$ As with method 1, $C>0$
A1: Awrt $k=0.386$ 3dp

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Using this value for $k$,

(d) find the population at 10 years from the start of the study, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Substitutes $t=10$ into $P=\dfrac{8000}{1+7\mathrm{e}^{-kt}}$ with their numerical value of $k$ to find $P$
A1: $(P=)6970$ cao or other exact equivalents like $6.97\times10^3$

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) Find, using $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, the rate at which the population is growing at 10 years from the start of the study.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Differentiates using the chain rule to a form $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{C}{(1+7\mathrm{e}^{-kt})^2}\times\mathrm{e}^{-kt}$. Accept an application of the quotient rule to achieve $\dfrac{(1+7\mathrm{e}^{-kt})\times0-C\times-\mathrm{e}^{-kt}}{(1+7\mathrm{e}^{-kt})^2}$
A1: A correct unsimplified $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-\dfrac{8000}{(1+7\mathrm{e}^{-kt})^2}\times-7k\mathrm{e}^{-kt}$. The derivative can be given in terms of $k$. If a numerical value is used you may follow through on incorrect values.
A1: Awrt 346. Note that M1 must have been achieved. Just the answer scores 0.

The population of a town is being studied. The population $P$, at time $t$ years from the start of the study, is assumed to be
